newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia warns Western states on trade issues.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia warns Western states on trade issues.

text.p: Indonesia's President Suharto, opening a meeting of southeast Asian economic ministers on Thursday, stressed that the World Trade Organisation should stick strictly to trade at its December meeting in Singapore.
"I would like...to emphasise that the World Trade Organisation should concentrate its attention more to concrete trade issues and not to divert its attention to issues beyond them," he said.
"The discussion on new issues which have not yet been thoroughly studied or are still untimely must also be avoided."
Economic ministers of the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) met to hear reports and discuss the region's fast-growing economic development.

ASEAN Secretary-General Ajit Singh said before the meeting the ministers would be "looking into the issues" before the World Trade Organisation (WTO) at its inaugural ministerial meeting in Singapore.
He said they would also review preparations for the meeting of the 18-member Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Manila in November.

Suharto said ASEAN -- Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines, Brunei, Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam -- should play an active role in APEC to help reinforce economic liberalisation and free trade on a regional and global basis.
ASEAN should also act as a bridge between Asia and Europe following the Asia-Europe summit in Bangkok in March.
"Based on the principle of open regionalism, we must gradually continue to develop and improve the most suitable means for ASEAN interaction with economic groupings in other regions," Suharto said.

Participants in Thursday's meeting said Suharto had sent a clear message to Western nations, such as the United States, that had said they wanted to raise issues such as labour conditions and rights at the WTO gathering.
"The statement was a tough one. People must take notice," one delegate told Reuters.

Most Asian nations, including Japan, say there are already mechanisms -- such as the International Labour Organisation -- to handle such issues. Emerging Asian nations feel they could be put at a competitive disadvantage in world markets if trade were linked to other such concerns.
"Hopefully, in the coming joint deliberations we should also take into account the domestic situations of the respective member countries with full understanding and sensitivity," Suharto said.
The ASEAN ministers agreed on Wednesday that good progress was being made in developing an ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) by 2003. The aim is to cut tariffs on most trade items to zero-to-five percent.
Suharto emphasised the role the private sector should play in regional development, adding that private business should also be involved in regional planning.
He also called on the ministers "to develop new initiatives for the promotion of small and medium enterprises that have great potentials in creating employment opportunities".
